BOUNDARY_1: n = 3 – the set \(\mathcal P_{3}\) has 6 points; the proposed three sunny lines miss two points.

CHALLENGE_1: The solution assumes “each non‑sunny line can contain at most \(n\) points of \(\mathcal P_{n}\)”. This is true, but later it assumes the three specific sunny lines will together cover **all** remaining points without verifying the collinearity of the leftover points.  
CHALLENGE_2: Implicitly assumes that the six points listed for the \(k=3\) construction are always exactly the uncovered points for any \(n\); this fails for \(n\ge4\) because the slopes chosen do not pass through the required integer lattice points.  
CHALLENGE_3: Assumes the three sunny lines are distinct for all \(n\); for small \(n\) they may coincide or become non‑sunny (e.g., slope \(-1\) appears when \(n\) is too small).

FLAW_2: **Lack of verification** – the solution never checks that the claimed lines actually pass through the intended lattice points; it merely states “one checks directly” without providing the check.  
FLAW_3: **Overreliance on a single pattern** – the same three slopes are used for all \(n\ge3\), but the pattern breaks as soon as the integer points no longer lie on those lines.

### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have not been able to produce a complete solution.  
I have rigorously proved that the extreme values  

\[
k=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad k=n
\]

are attainable for every integer \(n\ge 3\).  
The existence (or non‑existence) of configurations with intermediate numbers
\(k\) of sunny lines remains unresolved.

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Definitions.**  
   *A line is **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0\), \(\infty\) and \(-1\).  
   Let  

   \[
   T_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\}
   \]

   be the set of lattice points that must be covered.  
   \(|T_n|=1+2+\dots +n=\dfrac{n(n+1)}2\).

2. **Lemma 1 (Construction for \(k=0\)).**  
   The \(n\) lines  

   \[
   \ell_i:\;x+y=i+1\qquad(i=1,2,\dots ,n)
   \]

   are all parallel to the line \(x+y=0\); hence none of them is sunny.  
   For any \((a,b)\in T_n\) we have \(a+b\in\{2,3,\dots ,n+1\}\), so the point
   lies on exactly one of the \(\ell_i\).  
   Thus a configuration with \(k=0\) sunny lines exists.

3. **Lemma 2 (Construction for \(k=n\)).**  
   For each \(i\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) define  

   \[
   s_i:\;y=x+1-i .
   \]

   All the \(s_i\) have slope \(1\), which is different from \(0,\infty,-1\);
   consequently each \(s_i\) is sunny and the \(n\) lines are distinct.
   Given \((a,b)\in T_n\) set \(i=a+1-b\); because \(1\le a,b\) and
   \(a+b\le n+1\) we have \(1\le i\le n\), and the point satisfies
   \(b=a+1-i\), i.e. it lies on \(s_i\).  
   Hence the family \(\{s_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\) covers all points of \(T_n\) and
   contains exactly \(n\) sunny lines.

4. **Remaining problem.**  
   For a prescribed integer \(k\) with \(0<k<n\) we must exhibit
   \(n\) distinct lines, exactly \(k\) of which are sunny, that together
   cover \(T_n\).  
   The constructions above give the two extremal cases, but a general
   method that works for every intermediate \(k\) has not been found.
   The difficulty lies in balancing the covering power of the
   non‑sunny lines (horizontal, vertical or slope \(-1\)) with the limited
   ability of a sunny line to intersect many points of \(T_n\).

   At present I can state the following partial result:

   > **Partial Result.**  
   > For every integer \(n\ge 3\) the values \(k=0\) and \(k=n\) are
   > admissible.  Whether any other integer \(k\) with \(0<k<n\) is
   > admissible remains open.

Thus the problem is only partially solved.
